title: Buying Tickets Was Agony, and a Stranger Spent 40 Minutes Helping Me Find a Hotel | Traveling Without a Phone, Day 1
excerpt: I wanted my phone. Countless times.
body:
I wanted my phone. Countless times.

This is a trip from a slower era. I am pretending I have never heard of a device called a smartphone and don't know how to get online. I explained the point of the experiment in an earlier short piece; [click here if you are interested](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/14967.html).

The (intoxicating) rules:

1. I will take more than 4 kinds of transport and buy every ticket offline. I can buy the ticket to the next city only after I arrive in a city.

2. I will use as few electronic devices as possible (Kindle included). Each day I may write on my laptop for no more than half an hour, and the only website I may log in to is the QDaily back end. My editor may pick a reasonably doable task from the reader comments and leave it at the end of the previous day's article as my task for the next day. Please leave comments, even though I won't be able to read them.

3. I may borrow a stranger's phone or use a public phone to tell family and friends I'm safe, or to arrange to meet local friends.

4. I may carry a small GPS tracker of the kind made to keep children from getting lost.

5. This is not wilderness survival. The company reserves the right of final interpretation of these rules. Any resemblance to other experiments is surely no coincidence; it is tears.

Today is Day 1. I turned on my computer at 18:30, and my theoretical deadline is 19:00. The text I had written before September 26 runs to 1,807 Chinese characters, out of 3,666 in total. Because I couldn't bear to shut the computer, I am an hour late, and uploading the article took 5 minutes.

### No phone, so I packed these extra things

**Items: 8+; cost: 350**

![Items packed for a trip without a phone](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160606001728v6D10fOUJHYgKez7.jpg-w600)

Most of the time you barely notice how much this palm-sized thing does for you. Every time it lights up, it is doing some job. It is no exaggeration to say that without a phone you would have to buy a book just for reading on the toilet. Sad. Here is what I packed before leaving, mostly things a (lazy) traveler wouldn't normally bring:

A watch: replaces the phone's clock

A notebook and two pens: replace the phone's notes and storage

A children's anti-loss GPS tracker: replaces the phone's emergency alert

A camera: replaces the phone's camera

A paper book: replaces reading on the phone

Business cards: replace the QDaily app

Phone numbers copied out by hand: replace the phone's contacts

This list is not finished. There are many things I will buy when I get there, such as a paper map and a guidebook. I didn't bring an alarm clock, so I will have to rely on hotel wake-up calls.

### Buying tickets was truly agony

**Attempts: 4+; time: 4.5 hours+; cost: 1,704.5**

My ideal plan: Shanghai to Nanjing by high-speed rail; Nanjing to Qingdao by high-speed rail; Qingdao to Dalian by ship; Dalian to Shanghai by plane; and buy the ticket for each leg only after reaching the city before it.

As it turned out, a wish that beautiful was far too naive.

**Shanghai Hongqiao ticket purchase: failed; time: 2 hours+; cost: 0**

Five days before we set off, my colleague Xuan Hailun (the woman traveling with only a phone and no money) booked tickets to five places in a few minutes, right in front of me.

The day before that, I had happened to see a friend off on a bullet train at Shanghai Hongqiao, and was smugly pleased to have the chance to buy my ticket to Nanjing. To my surprise, the self-service machines at Hongqiao sold high-speed tickets only for the next 3 days, and so did the staffed counters.

**Jufengyuan ticket agency near Shanghai University: succeeded; time: 1 hour+; cost: 144.5**

With no other option, and somewhat crushed, I set out at 3 p.m. on September 23, under black clouds bearing down on Shanghai, for a ticket agency near my home. On the way, as I searched for it from memory, I saw a postal savings bank with the words "air ticket agency" displayed prominently at its door. My eyes lit up. I went in and asked: they didn't offer the service.

At last I made it to the agency on Jufengyuan Road near Shanghai University and booked a high-speed rail ticket from Shanghai to Nanjing, paying a 5-yuan service fee.

I asked the rather stern clerk to check trains from Nanjing to Qingdao between September 28 and October 3. "There isn't a single ticket left," she said, and added, quite harmlessly, "Buy plane tickets quickly, or there'll be nothing left. Too many people."

**Phone booking: failed; time: half an hour+; cost: 0**

I didn't know where the nearest air ticket agency was, so I thought of booking by phone.

I had two options: a public phone or a stranger's mobile. I decided to try borrowing a stranger's phone first and to look for a public phone if that failed. Luckily, perhaps because we were near a university, a young man who looked like a student didn't turn away the pitiful me.

I dialed 114, the information line everyone loves. After transfer upon transfer, that one call lasted 15 minutes, which made me feel terrible about using his phone. To book by phone you have to give your departure station, destination, ID number, bank card number and more, and the clerk reads everything back to you twice. It takes a long time.

The freedom of picking for yourself on a phone screen was gone entirely. All you can do is tell the clerk the time slot and other details you want. I wanted a flight from Dalian to Shanghai Hongqiao Airport, and a single sentence, "No tickets left, and the ones to Pudong are almost gone too," left me speechless. Normally I would try every trick on Taobao and Trip.com to snag a ticket, but now I had no choice. Booking by phone forces you to decide fast, in limited time.

At the payment step, sure enough, I hit a bug. I had never imagined booking by phone, so I had withdrawn all 2,000 yuan on my card in cash to take to the ticket agency. What was left on the card could no longer cover the two flights, Nanjing to Qingdao and Dalian back to Shanghai.

I didn't know whether to laugh or cry. That call was wasted.

**Phone booking: succeeded; time: 1 hour+; cost: 1,560**

After finding a bank, depositing money and borrowing another phone, I finally booked the tickets, in another call of more than 15 minutes. The kind, gentle clerk reminded me to note down the flight details, and only then did it hit me that I needed my notebook. My hand shook as I wrote...

The two flights are GS 7596 and HU 7370. My fares came to 1,560 yuan in total; on the Qunar app that day the same tickets totaled 1,340 yuan (all post-departure price comparisons were added by the editor).

What? The ship ticket? Let's talk about that once I reach Qingdao alive.

### It turns out Hongqiao isn't Shanghai's only high-speed rail station

**Time: 3.5 hours+; cost: 60**

Thanks to my own "assumptions" and my "bugs everywhere in life" constitution, things went wrong on day one.

I reached Shanghai Hongqiao railway station at 10:00 and noticed my ticket said "Waiting Room 7." Hongqiao has no waiting rooms at all. I realized I might have come to the wrong station, and I had: my departure station was "Shanghai Station," not "Shanghai Hongqiao Station." I rushed to the refund and rebooking window to return the ticket.

There I met a few fellow sufferers who had bought tickets for the same train. Here is a blurry photo, taken with a shaky hand:

![Fellow passengers who went to the wrong station, at the refund window](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606060017294jGbrTE8Jnd63uCD.jpg-w600)

After their refunds, they took out their phones, checked, found no tickets left to Nanjing, and bought tickets to Suzhou instead. I meekly queued for half an hour at the "same-day tickets" window, planning to take whatever came. The four or five people ahead of me were all going to Nanjing too, but there were no tickets; some changed their destination, others took a very late train. I was ready to leave in the evening when a handsome young clerk turned up a second-class seat on the 11:55 train. My savior.

With an hour to wait, I decided to eat something hot. I walked into the first place at the top of the escalator, a dumpling shop. A middle-aged man came to share my table. Seeing I had ordered only 6 dumplings, he scolded me: "Why are you eating so few?" I was sipping a hot soy milk with a flood of mixed feelings, and my eyes stung; I nearly cried.

![The man who shared a table at the dumpling shop](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606060017294mlPX6dcW2i0fZBV.jpg-w600)He said he was going home for the Mid-Autumn Festival

### Today I properly struck up conversations with 6 strangers

With no phone and no sense of direction, I followed my dad's rule: "The road is in your mouth" (ask). On the subway to Hongqiao, everyone had their heads down over their phones, sealed off as if behind screen protectors. I suddenly forgot where to change for Hongqiao, patted my pockets and found nothing to look it up on, so I asked an elderly couple who had boarded at Changping Road. They weren't staring at phones, and they cheerfully told me to change at Jing'an Temple.

My second conversation came on arrival in Nanjing, with a man in the food business who often travels between Shanghai and Nanjing for work. We stood one behind the other on the escalator, and he told me Fuzimiao might be a good place to stay: handy for sightseeing, and not as busy and noisy as Xinjiekou.

My third was a casually dressed, slightly plump high-school girl. Waiting for the subway, I overheard her complaining to a friend that Canteen No. 4 always oversalts the food. So I seized the moment and asked this picky eater: what's good to eat in Nanjing? She told me that Nanjing Dapaidang could meet most of a tourist's needs, and that there was one in Fuzimiao. My eyes lit up. I'll look for it tomorrow.

My fourth was two male college students as I got off the subway. I asked about hotel prices nearby, and they said they were a bit expensive.

My fifth was a cleaner I bumped into between the subway and the street. He told me the hotels were mostly to the right out of the station exit (this turned out to be wrong).

My sixth was rather moving. After turning right out of the station, I met a grandfather, 1.8 meters tall, carrying a few steamed buns. He walked me to 4 hotels over 40 minutes and helped me find a place to stay.

![The old man who helped find a hotel in Nanjing](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160606001730db7E38pa94TowgPN.jpg-w600)This old man made me love Nanjing

### "I thought he was your relative"

**Time: 1 hour+; cost: 794**

The old man told me I had gone the wrong way: the hotels were mostly to the left out of the station exit, toward the scenic area. He said there were 4 hotels over there that would suit me, and eagerly led me over.

The one he recommended most was a hotel with local character about 400 meters from the exit. He said it had good reviews, often had special-rate rooms and was great value. But when we got there, this grandfather, a local who almost never stays in hotels, found that only its restaurant was left.

We went back the way we came, toward where we started. Passing a 7 Days Inn, he took me in to look. Only a 250-yuan premium king room was left, and he suggested I keep comparing with the next two hotels.

Next was the Jinpeng Hotel: a single room for 278 yuan a night, breakfast included. He asked in the local dialect whether there was a discount for three nights, and the staff said they could drop the last two nights to 258 yuan each.

Less than 100 meters further on was the last one, a budget hotel. It was rather run-down, with a cramped lobby and tiny rooms, at 158 yuan a night. When I went to see a room, the guest next door was asking, "Why are all the plugs loose?"

I chose the Jinpeng Hotel. The old man said it was a lodging point for the Xuzhou Mining Bureau, so safety and hygiene were reliable. He wrote his phone number on a scrap of paper and left it with me. His surname was Hu. If I needed help, he said, I could call him; he lived nearby and could be there in five minutes.

The front desk clerk kept taking him for my relative, and seeing that I was traveling alone, printed me a copy of the "Nanjing Tourist Attractions Bus Route Map" without being asked. Sadly, the hotel has no airport pickup.

This is my room:

![The author's hotel room in Nanjing](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160606001730S3di82XNCtOc46rb.jpg-w600)

***Editor's note:*** *Booked on Trip.com on September 26, this hotel cost 248 yuan.*

### Today's spending

**Total: 3,102.5**

**How much I could have saved with a phone:** GPS tracker and other preparations, 350+; airfare difference, 220+; refund fee, 27+; hotel price difference, 30 (the editor also supplied these last figures).

**How many times I wanted my phone:** Countless.

### I'm stalling, so I can write a little more

1. This is my only way of talking to you. I have never loved writing so much, and I can't bear to close this page.

2. Check the departure station on your ticket carefully. Don't assume.

3. Buying tickets offline leaves you very little choice, but with luck there are pleasant surprises.

4. Without a phone, I feel like a vampire. Every emotion is magnified: happiness is happier, disappointment more disappointing.

5. An Easter egg: today at Hongqiao I personally lent a man 200 yuan to buy a train ticket. He didn't seem like a scammer, and he kept asking for my phone number. If I really do get a text when I'm back in Shanghai on October 7, I'll be very happy.

6. I'm off to find food. Goodbye, everyone, my dears.
